items.title: Molecular Prior Networks
items.abstract_or_text: Predicting affinity between small molecules and their protein targets remains one of the central problems in drug discovery. Due to the substantial cost of wet-lab experiments, machine learning models of drug-target affinity are usually trained on relatively small datasets, ranging from tens to hundreds of molecules. Given the inherent difficulty of generalization between different targets and chemical series, existing datasets of protein-ligand affinities are typically not used for new projects. At the same time, tabular foundation models, including Prior-data Fitted Networks, have recently shown how transformers can be used to solve machine learning problems in a single forward pass of the network, after being trained over a large corpus of, typically, synthetic datasets. Inspired by that line of work, we propose a novel affinity modelling approach, in which the labels of the query molecules are predicted from the labelled support molecules in a single forward pass of a transformer model. The model is trained on thousands of existing affinity datasets, enabling it to capture the general patterns of molecular activity across different targets, chemical series and dataset sizes. For the smallest support sets, our model matches the state of the art on the regression variant of the FS-Mol benchmark, while being faster than existing methods, thanks to the lack of task-specific training. A comparison against a reduced variant of our architecture, which amounts to kernel regression in a meta-learned feature space, shows that the predictive performance of the transformer model is only partially explained by simple molecular similarity.

items.title: A Machine Learning Approach to logBB Prediction Combining Molecular Docking and Quantum-Chemical Descriptors
items.abstract_or_text: Blood–brain barrier (BBB) permeability is a major challenge in the development of drugs targeting the central nervous system (CNS). Computational prediction methods can help prioritize candidate compounds and reduce the experimental workload during early drug discovery. In this study, machine learning models were developed to predict the blood-to-brain concentration ratio expressed as its decimal logarithm (logBB). The objective was to investigate whether molecular docking scores obtained with AutoDock Vina for P-glycoprotein (P-gp) and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP), together with quantum-chemical descriptors, could provide additional information for logBB prediction. The dataset comprised 685 compounds. A linear regression analysis identified eight factors associated with logBB: hydrogen bond donors, gas-phase electronic energy, electronic energy difference between water and hexane, number of heavy atoms, LogP, gas-phase geometry optimization time, number of aromatic rings, and fraction of sp3-hybridized carbon atoms. Notably, the electronic energy difference between water and hexane showed a stronger association with logBB than the corresponding Gibbs free energy difference, suggesting that electronic energy descriptors may provide complementary information. Higher-level quantum-chemical calculations will be required to investigate this finding further. Twenty-one machine learning models were evaluated. The selected support vector regression model using a radial basis function kernel (SVR-RBF; C = 0.869, ε = 0.135, γ = 0.165) was trained on 585 compounds and evaluated on a held-out validation set of 100 compounds, achieving an R2 of 0.605, an MAE of 0.368, and an RMSE of 0.459. Finally, the computational time analysis showed that descriptor generation was strongly dependent on molecular weight, with quantum-chemical calculations and molecular docking accounting for most of the computational cost. Overall, this work highlights the potential of combining physicochemical, molecular docking, and quantum-chemical descriptors for machine learning-based logBB prediction.

items.title: RxnMiner: A Multimodal Agent for Structured Reaction Data Extraction from Chemistry Figures
items.abstract_or_text: Reaction data underpin machine learning for reaction prediction, condition recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning, yet extracting these data from literature figures still requires substantial manual effort. Many figures encode multiple experiments through shared templates, substituent tables, and product grids. Recovering concrete reaction records therefore requires molecular recognition, association of evidence with individual experimental entries, and reconstruction of indirectly specified participants. We present RxnMiner, a multimodal agent system that combines an expert-informed extraction procedure with a chemistry toolbox to coordinate these operations. The agent reads molecular structures, resolves shared and entry-specific evidence, and instantiates participants from templates to assemble source-linked reaction records. We also introduce ChemRxn-Bench, a benchmark of 603 reaction figures with 8,547 manually annotated and reviewed reaction records, evaluated under a common protocol for exact molecular identity and reactant-product pairing. On this benchmark, with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next as the backbone, RxnMiner raises stereochemistry-aware reaction macro-F1 from 21.0% under direct prediction to 71.0%, compared with 25.0% for the strongest existing extraction system. Across five backbones, it also outperforms the same base agent without the extraction procedure and chemistry toolbox by 9.4 to 25.5 points. Applied without human intervention to 10,107 literature figures, RxnMiner produces a silver corpus of 88,202 source-linked reaction records.

items.title: El Agente Fármaco: A Scalable AI Scientist for Drug Discovery
items.abstract_or_text: Computational drug discovery offers a growing range of tools for proposing and evaluating molecules, but combining them and deciding what to do next still requires substantial expert effort. Here, we introduce El Agente Fármaco, an AI scientist that uses modern large language model (LLM) technology to turn discovery goals expressed in everyday language into complex, scalable computational screening workflows. The agentic harness selects scientific tools, reviews their results, and adjusts subsequent steps to the target and the user's objectives. Our approach centers on a shared scientific memory: Fármaco Atlas, which stores molecules, structures, and results together with their provenance -- a record of how they were obtained. The agent uses targeted database queries to retrieve the evidence needed for each decision. A single request can launch calculations for an entire collection of molecules, without requiring a separate LLM decision for every compound. This design limits the information the model must process as screening collections grow, while keeping the underlying results available for inspection and further analysis. The integrated tools support molecule generation, prediction of binding and molecular properties, and searches for compounds available for purchase. In a retrospective comparison with an expert-led campaign, the agent proposed chemically distinct candidates with competitive docking scores and higher calculated drug-likeness under explicitly imposed selection criteria. In a 22-task benchmark against plain tool calls and Codex, the agent achieved the highest observed mean model-judged score, with lower median cumulative token use and peak context. Fármaco provides a foundation for flexible, scalable drug discovery workflows that connect scientific reasoning with an enduring, traceable record of computational work.

items.title: DEEPNET-LLM: Highly accurate structure prediction of unknown metabolites from mass spectra via their molecular neighborhoods
items.abstract_or_text: Most molecular features detected by untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics remain unannotated. This so-called 'dark matter' currently comprises more than 90% and likely holds uncharacterized bioactive chemistry. Structure prediction from fragmentation spectra remains an outstanding challenge, because a spectrum does not uniquely determine a structure and the space of candidate structures is mostly unbounded; correspondingly, existing methods rarely return the correct de novo structure as their top prediction. Here we describe De novo Ego network-Enabled Propagation and Neighborhood Extrapolation of Topology using Large Language Models (DEEPNET-LLM) reasoning approach, which uses Molecular Community Networking (MCN) to restrict the search of a query spectrum to its local neighborhood within the global metabolome, and applies AI reasoning to propagate structural information from neighbors to the query. For a collection of 900 authentic standards (2,249 spectra) that have never been publicly released to exclude possibility of data leakage, DEEPNET-LLM returned the correct structure as its top prediction for 84.7% of spectra. Accuracy was independent of precursor mass across a range over which the number of candidate structures grows by 30 orders of magnitude, and was comparable across ion polarity, adducts and in-source fragmentation. On a random subset of the public MassSpecGym benchmark, DEEPNET-LLM reached 85.9% top-1 accuracy excluding stereochemistry. We showcase the use of DEEPNET-LLM with an example of a discovery of tryptamine amidate of a bile acid in mouse gut, confirmed against a synthetic standard. The DEEPNET-LLM approach is orthogonal to existing in silico methods and can be combined with them.

items.title: Guest-guest interactions and their impact on molecular mobility: a simulation study of 5-fluorouracil adsorption and diffusion in hydrophobic zeolites
items.abstract_or_text: Zeolites have been proposed as carrier materials for the storage and controlled release of the anticancer drug 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). Containing both hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor groups, 5-FU molecules can form relatively strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds. Prior work on zeolite beta has shown that guest-guest interaction between co-adsorbed 5-FU molecules reduce their diffusivity at high loadings. However, a systematic assessment of the influence of 5-FU oligomer size and zeolite pore topology is so far lacking. Aiming to fill this gap, the present study employs atomistic simulations at different levels of theory to elucidate the strength of 5-FU−5-FU interactions as well as their impact on diffusion in all-silica zeolites. In the first part, adsorption energies of 5-FU oligomers in four zeolites (FAU, BEA, MOR, MFI frameworks) are computed with dispersion-corrected density functional theory (DFT) calculations. In all four zeolites, 5-FU dimers are considerably more stable than individual 5-FU molecules due to attractive guest-guest interactions. However, an additional stabilisation of larger oligomers is prominent only for FAU, where the large supercages impose less constraints on molecular orientation compared to zeolites with channel-type pores. In the second part, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations with classical force fields are used to investigate the diffusion of 5-FU in zeolites FAU and MOR. For single molecules, the computed self-diffusion coefficients are on the order of 1 to 2∙10 −9 m 2 /s for FAU and 3 to 6∙10 −9 m 2 /s for MOR. Dimers and larger oligomers diffuse more slowly. While 5-FU dimers and trimers remain mobile in MOR, trimers and especially tetramers in FAU become nearly immobile on the nanosecond timescale. These findings highlight that the diffusion of molecules that can form strong hydrogen bonds can be significantly impeded by attractive guest-guest interactions, even at very low loadings. Besides, the low mobility of larger 5-FU oligomers could indicate that kinetic effects are responsible for the large discrepancy between experimentally reported 5-FU uptakes in FAU-type zeolites and theoretical predictions.

items.title: ToolSpace: Scaling Tool-Centric Environment Synthesis for Long-Horizon Agents
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models are deployed as long-horizon agents that compose diverse tools across MCP services into executable workflows. Existing MCP environment-scaling methods are data-centric: they first synthesize a database and scenario, then derive tools and tasks from them. As a result, tool interfaces may not match real ones, tool compositions are not grounded in execution, and tasks rarely span more than one environment. We propose ToolSpace, a tool-centric framework that reverses this order. ToolSpace mines data, state, and retry dependencies from adjacent calls in execution traces of real MCP services and open agent corpora, using deterministic rules rather than LLM judgment, and clusters the resulting weighted tool-composition graph into environments. Databases are synthesized only for state-mutating environments, while query and stateless tools replay recorded returns. ToolSpace then performs state-aware random walks with rollback and decompiles each chain into a natural-language task with assertion-based checks, keeping only samples that replay successfully from the initial state. Applied to AutomationBench and tau3-Bench Banking, the pipeline produces harder Pro versions on which 7 frontier models drop by up to 38.2 points. Across seven long-horizon tool-use benchmarks, ToolSpace raises Qwen3.6-35B-A3B from 23.0 to 41.0 average score (43.2 with RL) and GLM-5.2 from 44.6 to 56.6, on par with Claude Opus 5. Ablations show that execution-witnessed edges clearly outperform LLM-judged ones, and performance keeps improving with data and environment scale.

items.title: How Chemical Evidence Shapes Mechanistic Reasoning and Prediction by Large Language Models: Fine-Grained Inference in Nucleoside-Derived Supramolecular Gelation
items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) offer a distinctive capability for chemical problem solving by integrating chemical knowledge and experimental evidence through reasoning expressed in language. Yet how chemical evidence reshapes their predictions and expressed rationales is not self-evident and has received limited examination, particularly for challenging chemical problems. Here, using nucleoside-derived supramolecular gelation as a testbed, we systematically varied the evidence provided to LLMs and quantitatively evaluated their predictions and the mechanistic alignment of generated rationales. Without additional evidence, correct predictions were associated with greater alignment to literature-supported mechanisms than incorrect ones, suggesting that LLMs can draw on intrinsic chemical knowledge despite rationales remain largely general. Structurally similar gelation precedents, thought improved prediction accuracy significantly, reduced this distinction by anchoring rationales to insufficiently discriminative structural features, indicating that similarity-based evidence does not necessarily improve chemical reasoning and that prediction accuracy alone is insufficient to assess LLM performance in chemical tasks. In contrast, condition-constrained references and mechanistic information more consistently directed rationales toward chemically discriminative features, even when prediction accuracy did not improve in tandem. Together, our study highlights the importance of task-specific evidence design and quantitative rationale evaluation for reliable chemical problem solving by LLMs.

items.title: Accelerating antibiotic discovery from Earth's isolated habitats through protein language models and microfluidics
items.abstract_or_text: The antibiotic potential of Earth's isolated habitat microbiomes remains largely unexplored. Accessing this resource requires reliable prioritization across divergent peptide sequences and efficient experimental validation. Here we present MicroSPEAR, an end-to-end framework for antimicrobial peptide (AMP) discovery integrating SPEAR, a sequence-structure-aware ensemble predictor, with MicroGrad, a microfluidic testing platform. SPEAR generalized to low-homology peptides and prioritized potent candidates despite training on binary activity labels. MicroGrad simplified liquid handling and shortened susceptibility testing from approximately 18 h to 4 h. Applied to a catalogue derived from 4,480 metagenomes spanning 15 isolated habitat types, SPEAR identified 383,027 non-redundant candidate AMPs, 63.1% of which lacked detectable homologues in reference databases. Of 85 synthesized candidates, 79 exhibited antibacterial activity at [≤]64 M;. Mechanistic analyses revealed distinct modes of membrane disruption. Four broad-spectrum candidates with low toxicity significantly reduced bacterial burdens in a mouse thigh infection model. MicroSPEAR connects underexplored microbial diversity with experimentally validated antibiotic leads and provides a foundation for lab-in-the-loop discovery.

items.title: RxnScout: Deploying a Vision-Language Agent for Nickel-Catalyzed C-Glycosylation Condition Optimization
items.abstract_or_text: Reaction-condition optimization requires substantial experimental time and resources, making early candidate selection important when no target-specific yield data are available. Can pretrained chemical knowledge improve the use of the initial experimental budget? We evaluate RxnScout, a locally served vision-language model agent, in a wet-lab pilot to screen a previously unoptimized substrate pair in nickel-catalyzed C-glycosylation. RxnScout reads reaction-scheme images, selects candidates for testing from a chemist-curated set of commercially procurable reagents, and updates recommendations from measured yields. Sequential screening varies one condition dimension at a time, while a chemist reviews the accompanying rationales before execution. Wet-lab comparisons showed that RxnScout reached the best catalyst yield observed during the campaign (the campaign-best catalyst yield) in fewer trials than the baselines. We discuss deployment trade-offs, limitations, and errors in the generated rationales. A high-throughput experimentation (HTE) platform has been purchased, installed, and commissioned, providing the hardware foundation for the next deployment stage.

items.title: OperAItor: An Agentic Framework for Fault-Tolerant Operation of Chemical Processes
items.abstract_or_text: OperAItor, an open-source framework for developing and evaluating large language model agents for supervisory fault management in chemical processes. The framework is demonstrated on a dynamic reactor-distillation process representing isopropanol dehydrogenation, with physically based thermodynamics and modified reaction kinetics to permit liquid-phase operation. The process is represented by a 113-variable differential-algebraic model and operates at a nominal feed rate of 100kmol/h, producing approximately 4t/h of acetone. The simulated plant includes 8 PI control loops, 22 process alarms, 5 duty-standby pump trains, and 11 independent safety instrumented functions. The agent architecture integrates multivariate statistical process monitoring, fault diagnosis, knowledge-graph retrieval, action planning, and supervisory action generation. Five action-validation configurations are investigated, comprising operation without validation, an LLM-based judge, digital-twin simulation, and deterministic admissibility checks with and without consequence projection. The framework is evaluated using four LLMs across 20 scenarios involving single and multiple simultaneous faults. Without agent intervention, 18 scenarios result in plant stops, corresponding to an economic loss of 399,000 relative to fault-free operation under the assumed benchmark economics. For GPT-5 nano, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B, validated agent configurations reduce the number of stops to 5-8 and recover 265,000 of the loss. The study provides a reproducible benchmark for comparing agent architectures, language models, and action-validation methods for supervisory fault management in chemical processes.

items.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.

items.title: ToxINsight: An Integrated Web Platform for Sequence, Structure, and Ligand Binding Analysis of Snake Venom Toxins
items.abstract_or_text: Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank , AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models . ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/.

items.title: RGDM: Robust Graph Diffusion Model
items.abstract_or_text: Diffusion models represent a powerful class of generative models known for their solid theoretical foundations and remarkable performance across diverse tasks and domains. Existing node level diffusion methods synthesize nodes and edges within a graph, but are not designed to learn a robust generator from adversarially corrupted graphs. In this study, we introduce the Robust Graph Diffusion Model (RGDM), designed to generate labeled synthetic graph structures consisting of nodes and edges that integrate seamlessly into a given graph. The RGDM consists of a Robust Graph Autoencoder (RGAE) and a Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). Leveraging an edge selection mechanism and an innovative low-rank regularization on the latent feature, the RGDM produces clean and high-quality synthetic graph structures, even when trained on graphs subject to adversarial attacks. Comprehensive experimental evaluations reveal that Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) trained on the augmented graph, which is formed by merging the original attacked graph with the synthetic graph structures, exhibit significantly improved robustness against various graph adversarial attacks in the context of semi-supervised node classification. The code of the RGDM is available at https://github.com/Statistical-Deep-Learning/RGDM.

items.title: Scalable Contact-Gated Stochastic Operators and Universal Reduction Laws for Macromolecular Protein Dynamics, Allostery, and Kinetics
items.abstract_or_text: Constructing continuous, thermodynamically reversible reduced equations of motion from atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) that scale from fast-folding miniproteins to multi-domain allosteric enzymes in explicit water remains a foundational problem in computational biophysics. Across 15 molecular systems (890,000 SHA-256-verified frames, 0.89 us cumulative sampling) spanning 13 structurally diverse proteins from Chignolin (d=18) to explicit-solvent Adenylate Kinase (d=426, 40,110 particles) and Maltose-Binding Protein (d=738, 49,215 particles), plus two analytical verification peptides (d=2, 4), we formulate a contact-gated, GENERIC-regularized stochastic operator on the backbone torus T^d. We show that collective slow modes compress sub-linearly across two orders of magnitude in chain length - with spectral participation ratio scaling as PR(d)=1.061 d^0.494 (95% CI [0.332, 0.666], Delta AICc=-18.15) and short-time diffusion rank as r_D^90(d)=0.799 d^0.930 (Delta AICc=-14.39) - whereas cumulative 90% equilibrium variance in large native-basin enzymes transitions to extensive proportionality (10.0% blind extrapolation error vs. 35.7% for small-protein power laws). Consequently, macromolecular tractability above d>200 requires off-diagonal sparsity rather than global PCA truncation alone: universal peptide-plane crankshaft anti-correlation (mean R(psi_i, phi_i+1)=-0.603 +/- 0.054) and sparse 3D tertiary contact gating (mean k_eff=5.97, reaching 99.3% sparsity at d=738) enable a sparse directed acyclic contact-graph Cholesky estimator scaling empirically as O(d^0.92) in time and O(d^1.06) in memory (65.8x memory compression, 99.6x faster than Graphical LASSO, and higher blind held-out log-likelihood +0.303/d vs. dense +0.205/d on MBP). Biophysically, relative solvent-accessible surface area (rSASA_i) unifies dry linear equipartition in protein cores (alpha_core=1.00, 12.33% blind thermal error) with viscosity-coupled loops (alpha_loop=1.28) and peptides (alpha_peptide=1.57); parameter-free kinematic projection reproduces solution NMR Lipari-Szabo S^2 order parameters (mean r_s=+0.483 across four BMRB enzymes, Ubiquitin Pearson r=+0.921) and X-ray B-factors (mean r_s=+0.276); and 13-fold zero-shot Leave-One-Protein-Out transfer predicts unseen protein operators directly from static PDB coordinates (r_s=+0.706, R^2=+0.359 ridge; r_s=+0.721, R^2=+0.410 GBDT). Applied to functional discovery, explicit-solvent apo toroidal operators localize mechanical domain-closure hinges in AdK (PR-AUC=0.348) and MBP (AUROC=0.690 vs. 0.446 ANM), resolve distal Met20 FG catalytic loop coupling in E. coli DHFR (71.6% recovery at 93.2% sparsity) and beta1-beta2 Ile44 routing in Ubiquitin (7.1x amplification) on blind trajectories, and quantify sub-diffusive Mori-Zwanzig reaction-coordinate memory (mean gamma_M=0.593 +/- 0.126). A validation-tuned head-to-head benchmark against Markov State Models, TICA, Smoluchowski diffusion, Elastic Network Models, and unconstrained SDEs across all 13 proteins maps the physical regimes where continuous contact-gated GENERIC operators (lowest Frobenius error 0.288, exact 0.000 spurious entropy vs. median 65.79 kB/ns/d, IQR 53.76-104.66, mean 346.17) and discrete or harmonic baselines each excel.

items.title: CryoID2: deep learning-enhanced identification of protein and RNA from cryoEM maps
items.abstract_or_text: Identifying the molecular components of cryoEM/cryoET maps of endogenous or poorly characterized complexes remains a major bottleneck. CryoID2 addresses this by integrating deep learning-based feature prediction with sequence prioritization and structural evaluation. Three 3D U-Nets extract structure classes, key-atom positions, and reduced residue/nucleotide types from the input map. These predictions support backbone tracing and the generation of short sequence queries that rank candidates from a user-supplied pool-using BLASTp for proteins and a maximin strategy for RNA. Corresponding PDB or AlphaFold models are then retrieved, rigidly fitted using predicted features and experimental density, and ranked by map agreement. Module-level tests show high-recall feature prediction and resolution-dependent atom clustering, while a 52-case benchmark recovers near-reference fitting quality. In practice, cryoID2 correctly identified PfA-M17 from a 166-protein mass-spectrometry pool and the unannotated Ca-raiA RNA from a genome-derived non-coding sequence set, demonstrating a unified sequence-plus-structure route to molecular identification in cryoEM maps.

items.title: Large-scale AI-guided discovery of antifreeze peptides reveals functional tandem-repeat architectures
items.abstract_or_text: Despite growing demand for biocompatible materials that regulate ice crystallization in cryopreservation, antifreeze peptide discovery remains constrained by limited candidate sequence diversity and reliance on known protein scaffolds. Here, we establish an AI-guided discovery framework integrating multimodal antifreeze protein prediction, generative sequence expansion and local sequence-pattern analysis. AFPFusionLM combines protein sequence and structure-aware representations, achieving an AUROC of 0.937 and an AUPRC of 0.957 on an independent reference set. Antifreeze-domain-adapted protein sequence generation and multimodel consensus screening of UniProt, glacier metagenomes and generated sequences yielded 87,305 candidate protein records. Large-scale sequence analysis revealed recurring periodic sequence architectures across multiple candidate protein clusters, enabling the identification of short-peptide families with shared repeat features and their natural variants. Experimental evaluation revealed ice recrystallization inhibition activity in multiple peptides from repeat-associated families, with inhibitory effects comparable to or greater than those of reference peptides reported in the literature. Cell-based experiments using a representative peptide-containing formulation also supported its cryoprotective potential under reduced-DMSO conditions. These findings show that large-scale sequence exploration can reveal function-associated peptide sequence architectures, providing a research framework for the systematic discovery and subsequent optimization of antifreeze peptides.

items.title: How to Discover New Electrolyte Additives for Lithium Batteries: A Computational Roadmap
items.abstract_or_text: Electrolyte additives, present at a few weight percent or less, decide whether a lithium battery forms a stable solidelectrolyte interphase, survives high-voltage operation, tolerates trace water and HF, or resists fire. For three decades most additives were found by trial and error, and the few design rules that emerged, most famously “a lower LUMO than the solvent”, were known to fail almost as soon as they were formulated. Here we organize the computational literature on additive discovery, from the first quantum-chemical studies of vinylene carbonate (2002) to self-driving laboratories, chemical foundation models and LLM agents (2026), into a step-by-step roadmap: define the function the additive must perform; choose a descriptor that is actually predictive for that function; define and enumerate the chemical space; screen it with tiered quantum-chemical funnels; establish the decomposition mechanism; accelerate with machine learning; generate candidates beyond existing libraries; simulate the interphase the additive builds; and close the loop with automated experiments. For each step we summarize what has been established, what has only been correlated, and what has failed. We show that the hierarchy of redox descriptors (frontier orbitals → vertical and adiabatic electron affinities and ionization potentials → thermodynamic cycles → Li+-and anion-containing clusters → explicit-interface dynamics) is now quantitatively documented, that solvation-and product-level descriptors are emerging as the missing axes, and that the decisive bottleneck has shifted from candidate generation to reliable, fast, function-specific experimental labels. We close with a table of what each class of method can and cannot predict and with a realistic outline of a closed-loop additive-discovery framework.

items.title: MIMIC-Note-Extract: A Large-Scale Structured Dataset Extracted from MIMIC-IV-Note Discharge Summaries
items.abstract_or_text: MIMIC is one of the most widely used public hospital datasets for machine learning on electronic health records, yet clinically important information, such as past medical history, allergies, and diagnostic findings, remains confined to free-text discharge summaries. Studies requiring this information must therefore build their own extraction pipelines, duplicating substantial effort across projects. We release MIMIC-Note-Extract (MNE), a large-scale dataset that uses a hybrid extraction pipeline combining deterministic parsing with schema-guided large language model generation to transform 16 sections from 300,720 discharge summaries into structured tables. MNE adds information that has no structured MIMIC counterpart and enriches related tables with broader coverage and greater clinical detail, including 10 times more patient-history entries and medication histories for more than twice as many admissions. Validation by medical doctors confirms extraction accuracy above 92% across sections. Using MNE, we construct a clinical decision-making benchmark for LLM agents, demonstrating how reusable structured representations of clinical narratives reduce data curation effort.

items.title: Massively parallel quantification and prediction of monomeric protein yield in Escherichia coli
items.abstract_or_text: Obtaining sufficient quantities of purified proteins in their intended molecular states is essential for biological research and protein engineering. Advances in computational protein design have expanded the functional capabilities of de novo proteins and accelerated candidate generation. However, reliable methods for ranking expected monomeric yield of candidate de novo designs, including molecular binders, fluorescent proteins and enzymes, have yet to be established. Standardized measurements of monomeric yield across diverse sequences remain scarce, limiting our understanding of its determinants and the development of accurate predictors for candidate selection. Here we developed a scalable pooled assay combining peptide barcodes, size-exclusion chromatography and mass spectrometry to quantify monomeric yield for over 39,000 natural protein domain variants, de novo proteins and nanobodies under uniform and standardized Escherichia coli production conditions. We used this dataset to (1) quantify the relationship between folding stability and monomeric yield, (2) benchmark inverse-folding methods, (3) evaluate the utility of structure-prediction confidence metrics in selecting high-yield design candidates, and (4) identify sequence and structural patterns in nanobodies associated with monomeric yield and monomer-to-dimer yield ratios. We further developed ESMC-MonoYield, a protein language model fine-tuned to predict monomeric yield from amino acid sequence alone, and prospectively demonstrated enrichment of high-yield candidates among BindCraft-designed binders. Our approach enables standardized, large-scale measurement of monomeric yield across diverse proteins, and establishes monomeric yield as a sequence-encoded property that can be learned, predicted and ultimately designed.

items.title: A Latent Ability Model for Benchmarking Molecular Representations
items.abstract_or_text: The growing number of chemical foundation models calls for a standardized benchmarking method both for practitioners choosing representations and researchers identifying gaps. Previous work that ranked latent abilities of various chemical embeddings to predict ADMET properties suffered from significant shortcomings, including the use of biased datasets incongruent with real world usage and overstating statistically significant differences in model performance. We derive from first principles a variance inflation factor of (M+1)/3 for the Bayesian Bradley-Terry model evaluating M models on E endpoints at the exchangeable null and use numerical simulation to show variance inflation is still present in the non-exchangeable case. We propose a new method to directly model the margin of error as a function of latent ability and use it to evaluate models retrospectively on the datasets from the OpenADMET Polaris, ExpansionRx, and PXR competitions. We compare 35 embeddings and 13 end-to-end fine-tuned models across 17 ADMET endpoints. Although endpoint-to-endpoint variability means that no neural representation is expected to outperform ECFP on a hypothetical new endpoint in more than 95% of cases, our model concludes that 29 of 47 representations outperform ECFP in terms of latent ability with posterior probability above 0.95.

items.title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Generating HTML from natural-language specifications is an important application of code large language models (LLMs). Despite producing renderable pages, current models often fail to ensure functionality and visual quality during actual interaction. Existing methods typically target task-specific webpage supervision, leaving demanding interactive artifact optimization underexplored. Using mini-games as a challenging testbed, we expose limitations in interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment fidelity that are obscured by shallow webpage interactions. We introduce WebCatalyst, a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework with three complementary components: a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor for mitigating VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for grounding token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, predominantly for games, WebCatalyst raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and also the WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics. Further analysis shows that Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation, while runtime-grounded credit assignment accelerates functional improvement. Together, our results show that improving feedback fidelity is the key to substantially advancing interactive HTML generation.

items.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

items.title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning
items.abstract_or_text: Robust machine learning for graph-structured data has made significant progress against test-time attacks, yet certified robustness to poisoning - where adversaries manipulate the training data - remains largely underexplored. For image data, state-of-the-art poisoning certificates rely on partitioning-and-aggregation schemes. However, we show that these methods fail when applied in the graph domain due to the inherent label and structure sparsity found in common graph datasets, making effective graph-partitioning difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA), which enriches each graph partition with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges, enabling effective certification against node-label and graph-structure poisoning under sparse conditions. Our method is architecture-agnostic, scales to large numbers of partitions, and consistently and significantly improves robustness guarantees against both label and structure poisoning across multiple benchmarks, while maintaining strong clean accuracy. Overall, our results establish a promising direction for certifiably robust learning on graph-structured data against poisoning under sparse conditions.

items.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.

items.title: Molecular and Structural Characterisation of the MERS-Coronavirus Polymerase
items.abstract_or_text: MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus) belongs to the Betacoronavirus genus, which also includes SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of the COVID-19 pandemic. MERS-CoV is the pathogen responsible for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), a respiratory disease with a 36.5% case fatality rate. Given the capacity of coronaviruses for genetic recombination and mutation, MERS-CoV remains a pathogen of significant pandemic potential, with viral evolution potentially facilitating enhanced adaptation and transmission in humans. There are no approved treatments for MERS-CoV infection. The MERS-CoV replication-transcription complex (RTC), a multimeric protein complex key to genome amplification, has no cellular analogues and a highly conserved sequence, making it a useful target for antiviral compounds; however, structural and biochemical characterisation of the MERS-CoV RTC is limited. Here, we characterise the minimal MERS-CoV RTC using in vitro and single-molecule assays and show that it is susceptible to the RNA-dependent-RNA-polymerase inhibitor suramin. We present a structure of the minimal MERS-CoV RTC in complex with an RNA duplex, which shows strong structural similarity to the SARS-CoV-2 RTC. We use cross-subunit swapping experiments to show that the MERS-CoV NSP12 core can efficiently utilise SARS-CoV-2 cofactors NSP7 and NSP8, whereas SARS-CoV-2 NSP12 exhibits reduced in vitro activity with the MERS-CoV NSP8. This asymmetric cross-species compatibility highlights both the evolutionary conservation and virus-specific adaptation of coronavirus polymerase-cofactor interactions. Together, these findings provide a structural and mechanistic framework for understanding MERS-CoV RNA synthesis and establish its conserved RTC as a potential target for the development of broadly acting coronavirus antivirals.

items.title: Auditing frozen chemical language model embeddings for drug-delivery screening: fingerprint baselines, random-initialization controls, and scaffold-memorization control tasks
items.abstract_or_text: Frozen embeddings from pretrained chemical language models (cLMs) are widely used as features for ADMET and drug-delivery prediction, often with a linear probe and little validation of what the representation actually contributes. We audit two small public cLMs (ChemBERTa-77M-MLM and ChemBERTa-77M-MTR, 3.4M parameters each) on three delivery-relevant endpoints from openly licensed sources: blood–brain barrier penetration (B3DB, CC0), PAMPA permeability (NCATS via PubChem), and Caco-2 permeability (OpenADMET, CC-BY-4.0). For each endpoint we compare frozen mean-pooled embeddings with (i) Morgan-fingerprint linear probes with train-only tuned regularization, (ii) the same architecture with random weights (five initialization seeds), and (iii) scaffoldconstant control tasks in the style of Hewitt and Liang that quantify how much a linear probe can score by memorizing scaffold identity. On observed means, tuned fingerprint probes are slightly ahead of frozen embeddings on all three endpoints (paired per-split differences of 0.016–0.032 in AUROC or R2, smaller than split-to-split variation); trained embeddings exceed random-initialization controls by 0.04–0.10; endpoint probes are selective above scaffold-memorization controls, and the memorization ceiling rises with layer depth in the primary MLM model. Decodability of bulk physicochemical descriptors (molecular weight, TPSA, fraction sp3, aromatic rings) is largely preserved under random initialization, indicating an architectural rather than learned origin for those signals; learned increments appear for logP, hydrogen-bond donors, and rotatable bonds. We quantify three practitioner pitfalls: pooling choice changes endpoint AUROC by up to 0.05; tuning the fin- gerprint baseline’s regularization changes it by up to 0.03 AUROC or 0.20 R2; and scaffoldsplit construction details change means by up to 0.04, exceeding seed standard deviations. The source datasets are public and cited; all curation scripts, pipeline code, and per-seed results are included in the accompanying package. The study is compute-bounded to CPU and small models, which limits the generality of the conclusions to that regime.

items.title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
items.abstract_or_text: Language models increasingly serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as “The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is”, a small general-purpose model may answer “the alkyne group” instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models (a general-purpose base, three chemistry-trained models, and a reasoning-distilled model) on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether (R−S−R′) to thiol (R−SH), added to ether (R−O−R′), lands nearest alcohol (R−OH). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning acts less by adding this knowledge than by reorganizing it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

items.title: All-Atom Structure Tokenizer: AtomLM-9b for Biomolecular Structure Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: We develop an All-atom Structure Tokenizer that compresses biomolecular geometry into discrete structural tokens and achieves high-accuracy all-atom reconstruction. A hierarchical geometric encoder and finite scalar quantization map chemical units to a shared vocabulary of 8,192 tokens, while a joint coordinate de-tokenizer reconstructs backbone, side-chain, nucleic-acid, and ligand heavy atoms. The tokenizer achieves all-atom lDDT scores of 0.832 and 0.835 on CASP14 and CASP15, respectively. Building on this tokenizer, we train AtomLM-9b, an autoregressive language model based on Qwen3.5-9B that predicts structural tokens from molecular identities and connectivity and decodes them into complete atomic structures. We demonstrate, for the first time, protein structure prediction performance comparable to AlphaFold 3 with an all-atom-tokenizer-based structural language model: on the FoldBench protein-protein task, AtomLM-9b achieves a success rate of 75.01%, compared with the published AlphaFold 3 result of 72.93%. These results establish discrete all-atom tokenization as an effective interface between high-fidelity atomic reconstruction and language-model-based structure prediction.

items.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable SI Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
items.abstract_or_text: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generating novel AMPs with desired properties using generative SI (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable SI (XSI) methods to validate the GenSI model and derive biological insights. In this work, we fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. To advance the interpretability and reliability of the generative model, we applied Explainable SI (XSI) techniques. Specifically, we used a probing classifier and a regressor to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we validated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. Overall, these methods provide mechanistic insight into the model's decision-making process, offering a principled basis for trusting the sequences it generates rather than treating the model as a black box. Candidate sequences were filtered based on predicted Minimum Inhibitory Concentration (MIC) along with human insights into the structural activities of the AMPs in bacterial membranes, and a final set of peptides was selected for experimental testing. Biological assays for determining MIC confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, with fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements providing structural insight. With our XSI approach, we are able to reveal correlations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties of these sequences to bacterial membrane mimics, that directly correlate with biological activities in cell-based assays. This builds confidence in that the learned amino acid interdependencies as applied to AMPs carries physico-chemical meaning and is relevant for discoveries of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can serve as effective and transparent tools for rational AMP discovery.

items.title: Multi-Objective Generative Optimization via Expected Hypervolume Fine-Tuning
items.abstract_or_text: Scientific discovery requires plausible designs spanning useful trade-offs among competing properties: a molecule with strong binding affinity, for example, may be difficult to synthesize. Pretrained generative models, e.g., flow and diffusion generators, provide a foundation for proposing such designs, but steering them toward high-quality, complementary trade-offs remains challenging. Inference-time search incurs high per-sample costs, while fine-tuning typically relies on fixed per-candidate rewards that do not capture how designs complement one another. We introduce Hypervolume Fine-Tuning (HVFT), which adapts a single pretrained generator to maximize the expected hypervolume of its samples while controlling departure from the pretrained distribution. Expected hypervolume jointly rewards candidate quality and collective trade-off coverage. Nonetheless, we show that it cannot be expressed as the expectation of a fixed per-candidate reward and therefore cannot be optimized directly with standard techniques. A key observation of this work is that its first variation corresponds to the expected marginal hypervolume contribution of a candidate, which yields a tractable adaptive reward via an unbiased estimator based on model samples. HVFT uses this reward to decompose the objective into a sequence of KL-proximal scalar-reward subproblems. We establish concavity, relative smoothness, and convergence guarantees for the resulting distributional procedure. Across therapeutic-peptide and molecular design tasks spanning discrete diffusion and continuous flow-matching models, HVFT achieves state-of-the-art expected hypervolume and trade-off coverage.

items.title: An Expert-Augmented Deep Learning Approach for Synthesis Route Evaluation
items.abstract_or_text: Selecting multistep synthetic routes remains a major bottleneck in computer-aided synthesis planning because high-quality negative data are scarce and no single reported route can completely define route quality. We introduce an expert-augmented framework that combines large-scale reference-based route learning with expert-defined chemical feasibility assessment. Large-scale pre-training on literature-derived reference routes yields 60.3% top-1 reference-route recovery on held-out targets. The model’s rank-1 recommendations were feasible in 88.4% of assessed cases, comprising reported literature routes and expert-endorsed novel proposals. Expert assessment shows that disagreement with the literature reference does not necessarily imply chemical failure: 75.4% of novel rank-1 proposals were judged feasible. The pre-trained model already captures a measurable expert-feasibility signal (Spearman |ρ| = 0.46), which increases to 0.78 ± 0.05 after expert fine-tuning. On an independent multi-expert dataset, agreement with the expert majority increases from 48.0% before fine-tuning to 64.0% afterwards, compared with 64.8% agreement between a held-out expert and the majority of their peers under the same metric. Together, these results show that large-scale proxy supervision can provide scalable route prioritization, while limited expert supervision substantially improves alignment with chemical feasibility.

items.title: ProteoCraft: Protein Design as Proposal-Verification Search
items.abstract_or_text: Protein-protein interactions underpin nearly all biological processes. Yet, designing proteins with desired interactions remains challenging due to the structural complexity governing molecular recognition. This study views protein design as a search optimization problem over a combinatorial sequence space under expensive structural evaluation. Toward this goal, we introduce a novel tree-based search framework, ProteoCraft, that employs approximate structural gradients from diffusion-based structure predictors as effective proposal policies to specify where the search should explore. Complete no-gradient inference of folding models separately assigns values to the resulting sequences, determining what is good. ProteoCraft allocates this verification budget through a coarse-to-fine paradigm: multi-site edits first explore distinct sequence basins, then verified promising states undergo strict single-site refinement. Across fourteen de novo binder-design settings spanning eight target proteins, five immune-relevant TCR-facing targets, and four localized CDR redesign tasks, ProteoCraft improves design quality and high-confidence yield. These improvements persist under independent AF2-IG and Rosetta-based interface evaluation. Prospective experimental validation further yielded an 82.9% binding hit rate for PD-L1 miniproteins, with a best measured KD of 0.879 nM, and confirmed binding of designed IFNAR2 VHH. Our code is available at https://github.com/smiles724/ProteoCraft_v1.

items.title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
items.abstract_or_text: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.

items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.

items.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
items.abstract_or_text: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

items.title: LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately. Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. Agents frequently rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies only 1.4x. Models also adopt surprisingly different experimental strategies, and greater exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents often perform the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes, but still fail to use the resulting evidence. LUCA turns these hidden failures into measurable behaviours, providing a controlled environment to study where experimental agents succeed and fail. Code: https://github.com/RelationRx/luca.

items.title: Molecular crowding differentially regulates magnetic field-dependent fluorescence, recovery kinetics, and photostability of the magnetosensitive protein MagLOV2
items.abstract_or_text: Macromolecular crowding and solvent composition can alter protein conformation, diffusion, hydration, and cofactor photophysics, yet their influence on magnetically sensitive flavoproteins is poorly understood. We tested seven molecular environments in MagLOV2-overexpressing Escherichia coli lysate using a custom-built, high-intensity magnetofluorescence platform. Five-point concentration series of Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, PEG6000, PEG3350, glycerol, ethylene glycol, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were measured at 22 mT under continuous 6.12 W/cm2 blue-light excitation. Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, and PEG6000 progressively attenuated the negative magnetic field effect (MFE), whereas PEG3350 shifted toward mild enhancement at higher concentrations. Glycerol and ethylene glycol enhanced the negative MFE despite producing the strongest slowing of recovery upon the field being switched off (OFF-recovery), while BSA modestly enhanced MFE and accelerated OFF-recovery. Across 105 treatment cuvettes, the change in MFE was not globally correlated with changes in the OFF-recovery time constant (r = -0.07, p = 0.449). The initial pre-field illumination period revealed a second phenotype: Dextran and Ficoll increased late fluorescence loss, whereas glycerol and BSA were photoprotective. Pre-field fluorescence loss correlated moderately with MFE change across the full dataset (r = 0.474, p = 3.28 x 10-7) but not consistently within crowder classes. These findings show that MagLOV2 spin-dependent magnetofluorescence is shaped by crowder chemistry, polymer size, solvent environment, recovery kinetics, and photostability rather than by a single generic crowding or viscosity mechanism.

items.title: An Audited Open Record of Three Deep-Blue TADF Host Materials with Benchmark Tasks for Machine Learning
items.abstract_or_text: We present an audited measurement record of three phosphine-oxide hosts for deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF), with provenance metadata and benchmark tasks for machine learning. A scripted audit converted a 5276-file archive into 1662 files (1639 instrument files and 23 instrument-side fit tables) in ten record families, identifying 44 files stored under incorrect material or medium labels and retaining parsed settings, provenance tiers and quality flags. Colour recomputed from the spectra agrees with instrument reports, while gradient-boosted trees detect Raman-scattering artefacts in single emission spectra with a grouped ROC AUC of 0.92. Within-host interpolation is feasible, but three materials do not support broad property prediction for unseen hosts; the released scripts, manifest and task tables provide a reproducible baseline and a schema for adding materials.

items.title: DEL-Flow: AI-Driven Structural Generation and Activity Validation of MDM2-Targeting Macrocyclic Peptides
items.abstract_or_text: Macrocyclic peptides represent a promising modality for modulating intracellular protein–protein interactions; however, macrocyclic peptide datasets with reliable experimental activity measurements that can inform rational design remain limited. Here, we developed DEL-Flow, a pocket-conditioned generative framework for the design of MDM2-p53 inhibitors. Using an iterative DEL-selection strategy, a first-generation symmetric dimeric macrocyclic peptide DEL identified a half-scaffold associated with highly enriched library members, which was retained to construct a second-generation asymmetric focused DEL. Experimentally derived selection signals from this focused DEL were combined with computationally generated conformations and macrocyclic topologies for model training. DEL-Flow integrates these priors with MDM2 pocket and PackDock-derived pose information to generate side-chain variants while retaining the macrocyclic core. An SE(3)-equivariant flow-matching model generates all-atom coordinates, and a MASK denoising module predicts editable-region atom types, chirality, and bond connectivity. Starting from templates 126 and 319, DEL-Flow generated 20 candidates from each template, yielding 40 candidates in total. Following prioritization, 126-18 and 319-18 were synthesized off DNA and inhibited the MDM2-p53 interaction in fluorescence-polarization assays, with IC50 values of 1.95 and 6.50 μM and Ki values of 163 and 548 nM, respectively. These results support the use of DEL selection signals and pocket geometry to guide the generation of macrocyclic peptides absent from the original library that inhibit the MDM2–p53 interaction.

items.title: AlgoPilot: Cross-Paradigm Reasoning in Language Models via Strategy Selection and Guidance
items.abstract_or_text: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot.

items.title: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.

items.title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
items.abstract_or_text: Enterprises increasingly want LLM agents to automate standard operating procedures over their software stacks -- mapping each step of a procedure to the right call among thousands of internal APIs, without hand-authored step-to-API mappings. The core difficulty is API selection at scale: choosing and composing the correct tools over a long horizon, judged only by whether the overall task succeeds. Current tool-use benchmarks do not test this regime -- they expose only a handful of tools, evaluate single-step invocation, or grade multi-step behavior with subjective LLM-as-a-judge scores that penalize valid alternative trajectories. We introduce SLATE (Synthetic Large-scale API Toolkit for E-commerce), a large-scale benchmark that tests large-toolset, long-horizon API selection in a realistic enterprise domain. SLATE couples (i) queries decomposed into hierarchical, tool-grounded procedures over a ~1,000-tool e-commerce library, (ii) a deterministic, context-aware simulator that returns recorded outputs for matching calls and default responses otherwise, and (iii) an end-to-end task-success metric -- a task succeeds when it reaches every reference outcome -- that credits diverse-but-valid trajectories while remaining fully automatic and reproducible. Experiments with six open decision models and the language models they are built on, from 3B to 12B parameters, show that even the best model completes only 5.0% of the tasks, establishing SLATE as a challenging testbed for reliable enterprise tool use. We release SLATE, its simulator, and the evaluation harness at https://geshijoker.github.io/slate/

items.title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate non-pairing. These results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

items.title: Diffusion-Based Synthetic Pretraining for Root Segmentation in Rhizotron Images
items.abstract_or_text: Rhizotrons allow root system architecture to be studied non-destructively in soil. However, automated analysis of rhizotron images remains difficult: roots have low contrast against soil, soil particles resemble fine roots, and deep learning models need many manually annotated images that are slow and subjective to produce. Synthetic images could provide paired images and annotations at scale, but rhizotron images are largely absent from the data used to train generative models. We built a pipeline combining Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), ControlNet and inpainting to generate synthetic rhizotron images with paired root masks. We compared training on synthetic data only, real data only, and synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on real images, using three segmentation models: nnU-Net v2, YOLO26 and Mask2Former. Synthetic-only training reached a Dice score of up to 0.60. Synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the full real training set (two annotated rhizotron images) reached 0.80, and nnU-Net v2 and Mask2Former reached 0.62 with only two annotated image patches containing visible roots. When real annotations were limited, pretraining also improved segmentation of unseen crops, including lettuce, barley, wheat, maize, tomato, cucumber, French bean and field bean.
