We also introduced a Soft Dice score that compares predictions with probabilistic consensus maps from seven independent annotators, accounting for annotator disagreement. Models matched average human agreement on low-ambiguity patches but remained below it on high-ambiguity patches. In conclusion, diffusion-generated images can complement real annotations and help scale root segmentation, although their effect on downstream root trait measurements still needs to be validated.

items.title: Integrating Generative AI and Data Science into General Chemistry Laboratories
items.abstract_or_text: The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

items.title: Protein language models learn the underlying accessibility of mutations alongside protein fitness landscapes
items.abstract_or_text: Protein language models (PLMs) score the effects of amino acid replacements as pseudo-probabilities, which are widely utilised to map protein fitness landscapes. However, because their training data relies on natural amino acid sequences, these models conflate protein structural constraints with nucleotide mutation biases and codon accessibility. Using the rapid emergence of the divergent influenza A H3N2 K lineage as a stress test, we investigate how base PLMs (ESM-2 and ESM-C) versus fine-tuned versions of these models capture mutational processes. We systematically implement a parameter sweep to explicitly couple (or decouple) empirical nucleotide mutational supply from PLM-assessed amino acid substitution pseudo-probabilities across evolutionary forecasting tasks. We find that base PLMs implicitly learn generic nucleotide-level mutational constraints, an effect strongly amplified by virus-specific fine-tuning. Incorporating explicit mutational accessibility significantly improves the binary prediction of observed amino acid changes. Conversely, when predicting the final circulating frequency of variants that have already emerged, adding mutational supply degrades performance, confirming that selection dominates post-emergence dynamics. Additionally, we perform amino-acid-level epistatic scanning to investigate protein structural constraints in the context of genetic background. This indicates the improbable antigenic substitution I160K is dependent on co-occurring S144N and N158D mutations in the H3N2 K lineage. Ultimately, current PLM pseudo-probabilities are a composite metric that conflates protein structural fitness with historical biases in mutational supply. Explicitly decoupling these independent evolutionary processes optimises predictive accuracy for real-world pathogen forecasting and isolates pure protein fitness for synthetic design pipelines.

items.title: Glioblastoma model mouse rescue from mortality by brain-targeted catalytically-enhanced angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 mutant-antibody fusion protein
items.abstract_or_text: We have discovered that an engineered angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)-brain-targeted antibody fusion protein, referred to as ACE2dm-s1, improves survival of CT-2A xenograft glioblastoma (GBM) model mice when administered in combination with a small molecule STING agonist cancer therapeutic. Particularly striking about these survival results is that prior efforts that used losartan, a small molecule angiotensin receptor antagonist that acts on the same Renin-Angiotensin System (RAS) axis that is affected by the action of ACE2dm-s1, showed that this small molecule provided no survival benefit when used as an element of combination therapy in the same CT-2A GBM model used in our experiments. The improved CT-2A mouse survival, which was not observed for ACE2dm-s1 or STING agonist monotherapy, combines with our flow cytometry study results that revealed an ACE2dm-s1-mediated shift of brain immune cell populations toward an anti-tumoral composition to establish ACE2dm-s1's utility as a tumor microenvironment (TME) modulator that could serve as an adjuvant in increasing the efficacy of wide range of cancer treatment modalities including chemotherapeutic agents, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and CAR-T cells.

items.title: Xeno-Free Peptide-Functionalized Hydrogels Support hiPSC Encapsulation and In Situ Differentiation into Cardiomyocytes with Enhanced Structural Maturation
items.abstract_or_text: While defined synthetic substrates can replace Matrigel for human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC) culture and hiPSC-derived cardiomyocyte (hiPSC-CM) production, existing approaches culture cells on two-dimensional surfaces and yield structurally immature cardiomyocytes, limiting their use in disease modeling and regenerative medicine. Here, we developed a xeno-free, fully-defined cyclic RGD (cRGD)-functionalized alginate platform in which we encapsulated hiPSCs to support their expansion and in situ cardiac differentiation. cRGD functionalization was essential for hiPSC survival and pluripotency, with maximal support achieved at a low ligand density (25 M). In the presence of cRGD, hiPSC encapsulation into softer gels made from lower molecular weight alginates led to enhanced hiPSC expansion and improved cardiogenesis. Strikingly, differentiation in situ with 3D gels led to hiPSC-CM with higher structural maturity, including a markedly increased proportion of cardiomyocytes positive for the structural maturation markers Desmin and MYH7. Finally, after enzymatic retrieval from hydrogels, cardiomyocytes derived from softer gels formed tissue-engineered myocardium with superior contractile stress compared to tissue fashioned from hiPSC-CM derived from more rigid gels. Together, these results demonstrate the promise of this defined, tunable platform for biomanufacturing of structurally more mature cardiomyocytes from hiPSC.

items.title: The Limited Contribution of Structural Information Relative to Language-Model Signal in Data-Limited Cryptic Pocket Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Cryptic pockets, drug-binding sites absent from a protein’s static structure but exposed through conformational change, expand the scope of druggable targets, yet remain difficult to identify computationally. PocketMiner, a structure-based graph neural network trained on molecular dynamics simulation data, predicts cryptic pocket formation from a single static structure (ROC-AUC 0.87). Recent protein language model (PLM)-based approaches report further improvements over this structure-only baseline (up to 0.93), but do so by simultaneously replacing the structural architecture with a sequence-only model and switching to substantially larger, differently-sourced training data–leaving it unclear whether these gains stem from the languagemodel signal itself or from increased training data scale. We isolate this variable directly: holding architecture family and PocketMiner’s original, small molecular-dynamics-derived training set fixed, we compare three matched variants–geometry-only (baseline), ESM2 embeddings only, and both combined (fused)–under identical training conditions. The geometry-only baseline achieves chance-level test performance (ROC-AUC 0.498), while both the ESM2-only (0.817) and fused (0.835) variants perform far above it, with statistically indistinguishable confidence intervals between the two, indicating that language-model signal alone accounts for nearly all of the achievable performance, and that structural information contributes marginally under these conditions. This result is confirmed on CryptoBench, an independent, larger benchmark (baseline 0.494 vs. fused 0.716, non-overlapping confidence intervals), and holds consistently across every pocket-formation mechanism examined in a stratified analysis. These findings suggest that a substantial share of the improvement reported by prior sequence-based methods is attributable to language-model signal itself rather than training data scale, with implications for data-efficient strategies in structure-based pocket prediction more broadly.

items.title: Machine learning–driven inverse design of nanofiltration membranes for selective Mg2+/Na+ separation
items.abstract_or_text: Desalination brine, a byproduct of seawater desalination, contains valuable resources, including magnesium. Recovering magnesium requires selectively retaining Mg 2+ while allowing the dominant monovalent cation, Na + , to permeate. Nanofiltration (NF) membranes fabricated by interfacial polymerization are promising for this Mg 2+ /Na + separation, but their performance depends on coupled formulation and processing variables that are inefficient to optimize through trial and error. Here, we demonstrate a workflow integrating dataset curation, forward prediction, and inverse design of thin-film composite NF membranes. A dataset of 1,253 entries, comprising literature and in-house records, was cleaned, imputed, and augmented through chemically constrained permutation of interchangeable polymer, solvent, and salt variables in the training split only. Optimized extremely randomized tree regressors predicted pure water permeability, solute rejection, and intermediate membrane properties, achieving test-set coefficients of determination above 0.79. Shapley analysis indicated that permeability was governed primarily by formulation and processing variables, whereas rejection depended mainly on solute identity and charge, as well as membrane tightness. Using Bayesian optimization with a scalarized objective, two membrane recipes with favorable Mg 2+ /Na + selectivity were identified and experimentally validated. The inversely designed membranes exhibited the required Mg 2+ /Na + selectivity, demonstrating the capability of this workflow to design Mg 2+ -selective NF membranes for resource recovery from desalination brine.

items.title: From AutoResearch to Continual AutoResearch: Do Agents Learn Across Tasks?
items.abstract_or_text: Autoresearch has shown that agents can autonomously write code, run experiments, and iteratively improve machine learning solutions. Yet most evaluations start a new agent session from scratch for each new problem, making them costly and leaving unclear whether agents can retain and apply prior insights when adapting to new tasks. We introduce CONTINUAL AUTORESEARCH, an open-ended environment that compares persistent and reset instances of the same agent under matched task streams, data, and time budget. Continual AutoResearch covers nine task families, spanning synthetic tasks, symbolic regression, time-series forecasting, and tabular AutoML. Across five frontier agents, we measure first-solution quality, research efficiency, and final held-out performance. To distinguish insight transfer from session continuity, we run a memory ablation that vary what information agents retain from prior tasks. We show that persistent state improves research efficiency of all five agents, allowing them to find stronger solutions sooner. However, these gains do not consistently translate into better final solutions. Overall, our findings suggest that retaining experience and utilizing it effectively are distinct capabilities.

items.title: τ-Rec-Books: A Disclosure-Controlled Benchmark for Requirement Elicitation in Agentic Recommender Systems
items.abstract_or_text: While conversational recommendation systems provide a more natural user interface, they face the challenge of progressively discovering a user's needs before they can recommend an item that satisfies them. To evaluate the ability of AI agents at this elicitation process, we introduce τ-Rec-Books, a benchmark that holds each user request fixed while varying only when the user reveals their requirements: all at the start (volunteer), one at the start and the rest when asked (mixed), or some never (hidden). A hidden requirement can be found only by proposing books and inferring it from the user's accept or reject verdicts. We generate 450 tasks over a catalog of 20,000 books from Wikidata, develop a rule-based simulated user to answer the agent, and score recommendations against catalog metadata without an LLM judge. Across four agents and two search interfaces, success rates fall for every agent and interface, on average from 0.975 (volunteer) to 0.756 (mixed) and 0.283 (hidden). Mixed tasks fail mainly because agents do not ask, and when told to ask, every agent reaches at least 0.931. On hidden tasks, most failures come from agents recommending a book they never proposed to the user. When told to propose first, agents only match a simple baseline that proposes popular books, and stay well below one that uses rejection to rule out possible requirements. We release the catalog pipeline, task generator, simulated user, validators, reference agents, and all agent traces at https://github.com/nbharaths/tau-rec/tree/main/data/tracks/books-wikidata-v2.

items.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
items.abstract_or_text: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

items.title: SQLoom: Set-Contrastive Learning of Syntactic, Semantic, and Logical Dependencies for Text-to-SQL
items.abstract_or_text: Text-to-SQL translates natural language questions into SQL queries, enabling database access without writing SQL. Fine-tuning open-weight large language models (LLMs) is cost-effective, but existing methods treat SQL as ordinary text and optimize token-level likelihood without explicitly modeling its syntactic, semantic, and logical requirements. Thus, a single incorrect alias or comparison operator can invalidate a query while contributing little to training loss. We propose SQLoom, a constraint-aware fine-tuning framework with supervision at three levels: syntactic validity under SQL grammar and database schema, semantic alignment between query decisions and the question, and logical consistency across dependent clause decisions. SQLoom extends supervised fine-tuning with a unified set-contrastive objective favoring sets of correct outputs over minimally different incorrect ones at each level. LLM agents propose this supervision, which a SQL parser and execution on counterexample databases verify. We also release Spider-Refined, a training dataset correcting 378 flawed Spider annotations and enriching database schemas. Experiments on Spider, BIRD, and three perturbed Spider variants show that SQLoom improves execution accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B from 62.9% zero-shot to 88.7% on Spider development, reaching 89.2% on Spider test and 73.4% on BIRD development. It outperforms fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and agent-based baselines with up to 70 billion parameters. On question perturbations, SQLoom loses at most 0.6 accuracy points versus up to 12.1 for agent-based methods. It generates SQL in a single pass at 0.42s per query, 23\times faster than a GPT-4-based agent method. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of set-contrastive supervision over token-level training.

items.title: HLSClaw: Bringing Vibe Coding to High-Level Synthesis through Skill-Based Agentic Harness
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents are rapidly shifting software development toward intent-driven vibe coding, yet their effectiveness drops sharply in high-level synthesis (HLS), where code optimization must jointly consider design structure, directive search, and downstream hardware constraints. Existing HLS optimization approaches, including both heuristic-based methods and recent LLM-assisted pipelines, typically operate at fixed abstraction levels or in weakly coupled stages, limiting their ability to leverage the strong interplay between source code restructuring and directive search outcomes. Our key insight is that HLS optimization can be reframed from a fixed, hardwired transformation pipeline into a skill-based agentic control problem: an LLM agent equipped with modular, executable optimization skills and a feedback-driven orchestrator can autonomously navigate the coupled space of code restructuring and directive search. This motivates the design of HLSClaw, the first HLS-specific, skill-based agentic harness for holistic HLS optimization. On real-world HLS benchmarks, HLSClaw achieves a 39.12x geometric-mean latency speedup, outperforming the compiler baseline ScaleHLS by 1.98x, and surpassing the commercial coding agents Claude Code and Codex by 1.86x and 1.70x, respectively, while maintaining strong timing robustness.

items.title: GPU infrastructure for ML/MM with electrostatic embedding for enzyme chemistry
items.abstract_or_text: We present a fully GPU-native framework for machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) enhanced sampling simulations with electrostatic embedding, demonstrated on an enzymatic reaction. The framework combines a JAX port of the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model, an electrostatic embedding scheme compatible with the MACE-POLAR architecture, and integration with JAX-MD and PLUMED-JAX for end-to-end compiled enhanced sampling. The implementation is developed using GPT-6.1-Sol within Codex, with reasoning effort set to high. Using replica exchange umbrella sampling, we calculate the free energy profile of nucleophilic substitution in haloalkane dehalogenase in approximately 200 H100 GPU hours, treating the entire protein and reactants with MACE-POLAR-1-M-JAX and most of the solvent with molecular mechanics.

items.title: Design and Benchmarking of CK2α′-Preferring Inhibitors for Huntington’s Disease: The Limits of Structure-Based Isoform Selectivity
items.abstract_or_text: Protein kinase CK2 acts through two catalytic isoforms, CK2α (A1) and CK2α′ (A2), whose ATP-binding sites differ at only two hinge positions, making isoform-selective inhibition difficult. We tested whether a standard structure-based pipeline can design and rank CK2α′-preferring compounds. In a paired benchmark of 140 compounds measured against both isoforms, none of the five docking-derived criteria, computed with GNINA and convolutional neural network rescoring, correlated with measured selectivity (ρ = −0.19 to +0.12), and for matched pairs differing by a single linker methylene, the scoring reversed the experimental order. The only reliable determinant of preference, a two-carbon linker within the benzo[c][2,6]naphthyridine scaffold, was obtained from the measured activities rather than from any computed score. Molecular-dynamics ensembles of the two isoforms overlapped (0.88 Å between versus 0.72–0.96 Å within), placing the selectivity signal below the resolution of the methods. From an enumerated series, EV043 showed the largest end-point free-energy preference for CK2α′ (ΔΔGb -7.74 kcal/mol), although this value remained sensitive to the starting pose in CK2α, while the non-selective inhibitor CX-4945 was reproduced correctly (+0.08 kcal/mol). Distinguishing CK2α′ from CK2α therefore requires alchemical free-energy methods supported by experimental validation.

items.title: vibe-qc: expert-directed agentic engineering for scientific software development
items.abstract_or_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can implement scientific software, but useful development also requires executable comparisons, inspectable results and a record of scientific decisions. This case study examines the tooling that enables semi-autonomous electronic-structure software development under expert direction. VIBE-QC supplies molecular and periodic calculations; vibe-scheduler queues and manages calculations across clusters and a fleet of workstations; vibe-viewer and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) connect numerical outputs to portable inspection and reproducible figures. Retained development records illustrate how these tools preserve failed attempts, distinguish changes in physical conventions from implementation errors, and separate measured differences from expert-selected acceptance criteria. Publication-specific calculations were run with VIBE-QC 0.18.x and use formaldehyde to connect controlled numerical comparisons with visual inspection; diamond and lithium hydride provide periodic Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) examples with explicit convergence checks. The expert sets the physical problem, selects diagnostic controls and interprets the evidence; AI agents implement and execute those tasks. The resulting account identifies practical requirements for sustained AI-assisted scientific development. It establishes a traceable process within one project, without claiming autonomous scientific judgment or a measured productivity advantage.
